questions.stem: An ageing population is one in which:
options: the birth rate is rising, so that children make up a growing share of the population
life expectancy is falling, so that fewer people are surviving into their old age
the median age is rising and older people make up a growing share of the population
the total population is falling because more people are dying than being born each year
questions.explanation: Ageing describes a shift in age structure towards older people, measured by a rising median age or share aged 65 and over. A population can age while still growing, so decline is not part of the definition.

questions.stem: The two main causes of population ageing are:
options: high infant mortality and large-scale immigration
rising birth rates and the emigration of older people
sustained low fertility and rising life expectancy
sustained high fertility and falling life expectancy
questions.explanation: Fewer births shrink the younger age groups, while longer lives enlarge the older ones. High fertility and falling life expectancy would make a population younger, not older.

questions.stem: A country with a growing population and high fertility typically has:
options: a high youth dependency ratio
a high old-age dependency ratio
a median age above 45 years
a population pyramid with a narrow base
questions.explanation: High fertility produces large numbers of children, so there are many people under 15 for each person of working age. A high old-age ratio and a narrow base are features of ageing populations.

questions.stem: The old-age dependency ratio is the number of people aged:
options: 0 to 14 and 65 and over per 100 people aged 15 to 64
15 to 64 per 100 people aged 65 and over
65 and over per 100 people aged 15 to 64
65 and over per 100 people in the whole population
questions.explanation: The old-age dependency ratio compares older people with the working-age population. Including those aged 0 to 14 gives the total dependency ratio.

questions.stem: A hypothetical country has 30 million people aged 65 and over and 75 million aged 15 to 64. Its old-age dependency ratio is:
questions.explanation: Divide 30 million by 75 million and multiply by 100 to get 40 older people per 100 of working age. Dividing 75 by 30 gives 2.5, which is the number of working-age people per older person, not the ratio.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical country with a stable total population, the old-age dependency ratio rose from 20 to 50 per 100 over 40 years. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There are now 2.5 times as many older people per working-age person, adding pressure on taxes
Half of the country's population is now aged 65 and over, so most people are retired
The total population has more than doubled, mainly through the growth of the older age groups
The working-age population has grown, so each worker now supports fewer older people
questions.explanation: A ratio of 50 per 100 means one older person for every two people aged 15 to 64, up from one for every five, so each worker supports more retirees through taxes. It does not mean half the whole population is old, because children are also part of the population.

questions.stem: Which is an issue that commonly results from a rapidly growing, youthful population?
options: Too few children to keep schools open in many towns and suburbs
Demand for schools, health care and jobs growing faster than they can be provided
A shrinking workforce that cannot pay for the pensions of a large retired population
Large numbers of vacant houses in rural villages as the population falls
questions.explanation: Each year more children need school places and, later, more young adults need jobs, which can outpace investment in services. Vacant houses, closing schools and a shrinking workforce are issues of ageing and declining populations.

questions.stem: In many fast-growing cities of developing countries, a common challenge arising from rapid population growth is:
options: the closure of maternity hospitals because too few babies are being born
a rapid fall in the demand for public transport as the city's population ages
informal settlements growing faster than water, sanitation and housing can be provided
a shortage of young workers to fill the jobs created by new factories and offices
questions.explanation: Natural increase and rural-to-urban migration can add people faster than governments can build housing and services, so many people live in informal settlements. A shortage of young workers is a challenge of ageing, not growth.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental issue that can result from a rapidly growing rural population?
options: Abandonment of terraced fields and their reversion to scrub as farmers age
A fall in the demand for firewood and timber for building houses
Reduced pressure on water supplies as the number of farms declines
Clearing of forest and overuse of farmland, leading to soil degradation
questions.explanation: More people need more land, water and fuel, which can lead to clearing, shorter fallow periods and soil degradation. Abandoned farmland is associated with rural depopulation and ageing.

questions.stem: A country's fertility has begun to fall, so in 20 years the share of its people of working age will be much larger. This could produce a demographic dividend only if:
options: there are enough jobs, education and health care for the larger workforce to be productive
the birth rate rises again to restore the high proportion of children in the population
the extra workers emigrate, so that the remaining population has more land and food
the government raises the pension age so that young people cannot enter the paid workforce
questions.explanation: A falling dependency ratio gives a window in which more workers support fewer dependants, but the benefit depends on employing them productively. Without jobs, a large working-age population can instead mean high youth unemployment.

questions.stem: In a growing country, infant mortality falls sharply while fertility stays high. Which challenge is most likely about 15 to 20 years later?
options: A shortage of older people to fill the places available in the country's aged care homes
A fall in the number of people needing secondary school places
A rapid rise in the share of the population aged 65 and over
Many more young people entering the labour market, increasing the demand for jobs
questions.explanation: More surviving children means larger groups reach working age after about 15 to 20 years, so the challenge moves from schooling to employment. A rise in the share aged 65 and over comes much later, after fertility falls.

questions.stem: Which is an economic issue that commonly results from an ageing population?
options: Rising spending on new primary schools as the number of children increases
High youth unemployment as large numbers of young people seek work
Rapid growth in informal settlements on the edges of the country's largest cities
Rising spending on pensions and health care while the share of taxpayers falls
questions.explanation: Older people draw more on pensions and health services, while a shrinking share of working-age people pays most income tax. Youth unemployment and the need for new schools are issues of youthful, growing populations.

questions.stem: In many rural areas of Japan, young people moving to cities combined with an ageing population has led to:
options: a shortage of farmland because so many young people want to take up farming
abandoned houses, closing schools and the withdrawal of shops and services
rapid growth in the number of new primary schools and maternity clinics
overcrowding in rural housing as families grow larger each generation
questions.explanation: Out-migration of the young leaves elderly residents behind, and as numbers fall, schools close, houses are left empty (akiya) and services are withdrawn. The other options describe the effects of a young, growing population.

questions.stem: Which is a social issue resulting from an ageing population?
options: More older people living alone and needing care, with fewer family members to provide it
Higher government spending on age pensions funded by a smaller share of taxpayers
A shrinking labour force that slows the country's rate of economic growth and its tax revenue
Higher taxes on goods and services to fund the costs of health care
questions.explanation: Social issues concern people's wellbeing, families and communities, such as isolation and the availability of carers. Pension spending, labour force decline and taxes are economic issues.

questions.stem: China's one-child policy, introduced around 1980, is an example of:
options: a pronatalist policy, designed to raise the birth rate
an immigration policy, designed to increase the workforce
a pension policy, designed to support the elderly
an antinatalist policy, designed to lower the birth rate
questions.explanation: Antinatalist policies aim to reduce fertility, and the one-child policy limited most urban couples to a single child. Pronatalist policies encourage births.

questions.stem: Which statement about China's one-child policy is accurate?
options: It applied identically to every family in every province from the beginning
It allowed every couple two children, provided they lived in a rural area
It was abolished in the late 1980s after a sharp and unexpected fall in the national death rate
Rules varied: many rural couples could have a second child if the first was a girl
questions.explanation: The policy applied most strictly to urban Han Chinese couples; many rural families could have a second child if the first was a daughter, and ethnic minorities faced looser limits. It was replaced by a universal two-child policy in 2016.

questions.stem: The '4-2-1' problem linked to China's one-child policy describes:
options: four children in each family who must share the care of two parents and one grandparent
a ratio of four workers for every two retirees and one child in the population
four provinces with two-child rules for every one province with one-child rules
one adult child who may be responsible for two parents and four grandparents
questions.explanation: With only children in two successive generations, a single adult may have two ageing parents and four grandparents depending on them. This intensifies the challenge of caring for an ageing population.

questions.stem: A preference for sons combined with the one-child policy contributed to which challenge in China?
options: A surplus of young men relative to young women of marriageable age
A surplus of young women relative to young men of marriageable age
A rise in the total fertility rate to well above replacement level
A fall in the median age of the population from the 1980s onwards
questions.explanation: With only one child allowed, some families used sex-selective abortion or abandoned girls, so the sex ratio at birth became strongly male-biased. The policy lowered fertility and raised the median age, the opposite of the other options.

questions.stem: China's total fertility rate fell by about half during the 1970s, before the one-child policy began. In evaluating the policy, this suggests that:
options: the one-child policy caused the fall in fertility during the 1970s as well
the policy had no effect at all on fertility in the decades after it was introduced
fertility in China was rising rapidly when the policy was introduced
not all of the later fall in fertility can be credited to the one-child policy
questions.explanation: Earlier campaigns promoting later marriage, longer spacing and fewer children, together with development, had already cut fertility sharply, so the policy's own effect is hard to separate. That does not mean it had no effect, only that it was not the sole cause.

questions.stem: China replaced the one-child policy with a universal two-child policy in 2016 mainly because of concern about:
options: rising unemployment among young university graduates
a surplus of women in the working-age groups
rapid ageing and a shrinking working-age population
a rising birth rate and a growing shortage of food
questions.explanation: Decades of low fertility left China with a rapidly growing older population and a falling number of working-age people. The concern was too few births, not too many.

questions.stem: Strategies that keep girls in secondary school tend to reduce fertility because educated women:
options: are required by law to have fewer children than women who have left school early
are more likely to live in rural areas, where families are usually smaller than in cities
have higher infant mortality, so fewer of their children survive to adulthood
tend to marry later, know more about contraception and have more paid work options
questions.explanation: Education delays marriage and first births, increases knowledge of and access to family planning, and raises the value of women's time in paid work. Educated women's children are more likely to survive, not less.

questions.stem: An NGO trains community health workers to provide contraception and maternal health advice in rural villages. Which is the most appropriate measure of its effectiveness?
options: The number of health workers who enrolled in the training course in the program's first month
Whether the program was praised by politicians in the country's capital city at its launch
Change in contraceptive use and fertility in villages served compared with similar villages not served
The total amount of money the NGO spent on the program during its first year of operation
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is about outcomes, so the best criterion compares results in villages with and without the program. Money spent and workers enrolled are inputs, which show effort rather than results.

questions.stem: Which is a non-government strategy in response to the issues of a growing population?
options: An NGO running mobile family planning clinics in remote districts
A national law setting the minimum age of marriage at 18 years
A government program building secondary schools in rural areas
A national census used to plan the location of new hospitals
questions.explanation: Non-government organisations, such as international family planning charities, often deliver services where governments cannot reach. Laws, government school programs and censuses are government strategies.

questions.stem: A government responds to rapid urban growth by bulldozing informal settlements and moving residents to new housing 40 km from the city. Which is the most likely negative impact?
options: Residents' access to urban employment improves because of the new housing
The informal settlements grow larger because the government has improved them
Residents lose access to their jobs and social networks in the city
The city's population grows faster because more housing is available
questions.explanation: Relocating people far from where they work and have family and community ties can increase poverty and travel costs even if the housing is better. Improved access to jobs would be a positive impact, and it is unlikely from a site so far away.

questions.stem: A government offers a cash payment for each new baby born. This is an example of:
options: an antinatalist strategy
an immigration strategy
a retirement strategy
a pronatalist strategy
questions.explanation: Pronatalist strategies encourage people to have more children, which responds to low fertility in ageing countries. An antinatalist strategy, such as the one-child policy, discourages births.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical country, births rose 6% in the two years after a cash payment for each birth was introduced, then fell back to the earlier level. Which evaluation is best supported?
options: The payment had no effect at all, because births eventually returned to their earlier level
The payment may have changed the timing of births more than the number of children families had
The payment permanently raised fertility, because births rose immediately after it was introduced
The payment caused births to fall, because births were lower at the end than in the second year
questions.explanation: A short-lived rise that then falls back suggests some parents had children sooner rather than having more children overall. The rise shows the payment had some effect, so 'no effect at all' overstates the case.

questions.stem: Which strategy addresses a key cause of low fertility in ageing countries where many women are in paid work?
options: Increasing the number of aged care places available in residential homes
Affordable childcare and paid parental leave that make it easier to combine work and family
Reducing the number of places available for women in universities and technical colleges
Raising the age at which people can receive the age pension from the government
questions.explanation: When combining work and children is difficult, many couples delay or limit births, so childcare and parental leave target that barrier. Raising the pension age and adding aged care places respond to ageing but do not affect fertility.

questions.stem: Raising the age at which people can receive a government age pension responds to an ageing population by:
options: increasing the birth rate by giving young couples more time to have children
lowering life expectancy so that people receive pensions for a shorter period
attracting young immigrants who will pay taxes to fund the pension system
keeping people in the workforce longer and reducing the number receiving pensions
questions.explanation: A higher pension age, such as Australia's rise to 67, means people are paid the pension for fewer years and many work longer and pay tax. It does not change fertility or attract migrants.

questions.stem: Australia's compulsory superannuation, in which employers pay a share of wages into workers' retirement savings, responds to ageing by:
options: increasing the number of babies born to working parents
lowering the age at which people can stop working
reducing the number of migrants needed each year
reducing future reliance on the government age pension
questions.explanation: Superannuation builds private savings for retirement, so fewer retirees depend fully on the tax-funded pension. It is a strategy for the costs of ageing, not for fertility or migration.

questions.stem: Why does a skilled migration program slow population ageing?
options: Skilled migrants are required by law to have more children than people born locally
Older residents must leave the country to make room for the incoming migrants
Migrants are not counted in the population, so the median age appears lower
Most skilled migrants are young adults of working age, which lowers the median age
questions.explanation: Skilled visas favour people in their twenties and thirties, who add to the working-age population and pay taxes. Migrants are counted in the population, and they are not required to have children.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest limitation of relying on immigration to prevent population ageing?
options: Migrants also age, so very large and continuing intakes would be needed to keep the structure stable
Migrants are not permitted to work in health and aged care, so they cannot help with the challenges
Migrants always return to their home countries before they reach the age of retirement
Immigration raises the median age immediately, because most migrants are over 65 when they arrive
questions.explanation: Immigration can slow ageing, but migrants grow older too, so holding the age structure steady would require ever-larger intakes. Many migrants work in health and aged care, and most arrive at working ages, not over 65.

questions.stem: Japan introduced a Specified Skilled Worker visa in 2019. This strategy was a response to:
options: labour shortages in sectors such as aged care and construction as the workforce shrinks
rising unemployment among young Japanese workers caused by rapid population growth
a rapid increase in Japan's birth rate that left too few places in schools
a large surplus of workers in Japan's farming and fishing industries
questions.explanation: With its working-age population falling, Japan opened new visa pathways for foreign workers in sectors short of labour, including nursing care. Japan's challenge is too few workers, not rapid population growth.

questions.stem: In Japan, robots and assistive technologies are being developed for aged care mainly because:
options: aged care homes in Japan are closing as the number of older people falls
there are too few care workers for the growing number of older people
older people in Japan are not allowed to be cared for by other people
the birth rate is rising, so more workers are needed in childcare
questions.explanation: Rising numbers of very old people and a shrinking workforce create a gap in care, which technology aims to help fill. The number of older people in Japan is rising, not falling.

questions.stem: Japan raised its consumption tax partly to fund social security for its ageing population. Which is an economic impact of this strategy on people?
options: The birth rate rises because children are exempt from tax
Life expectancy falls because health care becomes cheaper
Households pay higher prices for many goods and services
Older people receive smaller pensions as a direct result
questions.explanation: A consumption tax is added to the price of goods and services, so households pay more, while the revenue supports pensions and health care. Raising the tax increased funds for older people rather than cutting their pensions.

questions.stem: Placing Japan's ageing population in its world regional context shows that:
options: Japan's neighbours all have rapidly growing, youthful populations with high fertility
ageing in East Asia is caused mainly by the emigration of older people to Japan
very low fertility and rapid ageing are shared by neighbours such as South Korea and China
Japan is the only country in East Asia whose fertility has fallen below replacement level
questions.explanation: South Korea, Taiwan and China also have fertility well below replacement and are ageing rapidly, so Japan's trend is part of a regional pattern. Japan is not alone, and its neighbours do not have high fertility.

questions.stem: Within Nigeria, fertility is generally higher in the northern states than in the south. This pattern is most likely to be spatially associated with:
options: a policy in the southern states that limits each family to two children by law
lower rates of female education and higher rates of early marriage in the north
higher rates of female education and later marriage in the northern states
higher incomes and better access to health care in the northern states
questions.explanation: Survey data show the north has lower female school attendance and earlier marriage, both associated with higher fertility. There is no two-child limit in southern Nigeria.

questions.stem: Within an ageing country such as Australia, the highest proportions of older people are often found in:
options: new housing estates on the fringes of the capital cities
mining towns with many young workers on fly-in fly-out rosters in remote regions
rural areas young people have left and coastal towns popular with retirees
inner-city suburbs with many universities and student apartments
questions.explanation: Out-migration of young adults and in-migration of retirees raise the share of older people in rural and coastal 'sea change' towns. New fringe estates and student areas attract young families and students.

questions.stem: Many retirees move from a capital city to a coastal town. This population movement contributes to structural change in the town by:
options: raising the town's birth rate as new families settle in the area
reducing the town's population as residents leave to make room for retirees
raising the median age and the demand for health and aged care services
lowering the median age and the demand for primary schools and childcare
questions.explanation: An inflow of older people enlarges the top of the town's pyramid, raising the median age and changing the services needed. Retirees do not raise the birth rate.

questions.stem: A student says that food insecurity in a fast-growing region is caused solely by population growth. The best response is that:
options: food insecurity cannot occur where population is growing, because there are more farmers
other causes, such as drought, conflict and poor transport, also contribute to food insecurity
population growth has no connection at all to food insecurity in any region of the world
food insecurity is caused only by population ageing, not by population growth
questions.explanation: Population growth increases demand, but issues usually have several causes, including climate, conflict, poverty and infrastructure. Saying growth has no connection at all overstates the case in the other direction.

questions.stem: Which factor contributing to high fertility is best classified as cultural?
options: A lack of health clinics in remote rural districts
A tradition that values large families as a sign of status and blessing
Children working on family farms to provide labour and income
A government ban on the import and sale of contraceptives in the country
questions.explanation: Cultural factors concern values, beliefs and traditions. Child labour on farms is an economic factor, a government ban is political, and a lack of clinics relates to social services and infrastructure.

questions.stem: A state government overlays a GIS map of residents aged 80 and over with travel times to hospitals and aged care homes. The main use of this analysis is to:
options: count the exact number of people aged 80 and over who will need care next year
measure the life expectancy of the residents of each suburb in the state
record the names and addresses of older residents who are living alone
identify areas where services are lacking, to plan where new facilities should go
questions.explanation: Overlaying where older people live on access to services shows gaps, helping governments locate new facilities where they are most needed. GIS maps patterns; it does not forecast exact individual needs or measure life expectancy.

questions.stem: In a fast-growing country where census data are out of date, high-resolution satellite imagery can support strategies by:
options: estimating where settlements and people are, so health and vaccination campaigns reach them
recording the age and sex of every person living in each building in the country
replacing the need for any health workers to visit communities on the ground
measuring the fertility rate of women in each village from the number of roofs
questions.explanation: Mapping buildings from imagery helps planners estimate where people live, so teams and supplies can be sent to every settlement. Imagery cannot show who lives in a building, so ground surveys are still needed.

questions.stem: Which is the main limitation of satellite imagery in planning strategies for population issues?
options: It can be used only in developed countries, because satellites do not pass over developing ones
It cannot show settlements at all, because buildings are too small to see from space
It is always out of date, because satellites take a new image of each place only once a decade
It shows buildings and land use but not the number, ages or needs of the people within them
questions.explanation: Imagery reveals the built environment, but planners also need demographic and survey data to know who lives there and what they need. Modern satellites image most places frequently and can resolve individual buildings.
